query: Which method can be used for phase stability, microstructure refinement, and property optimization, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Implementing a CALPHAD‐based high‐throughput computational screening method in high-entropy alloy (HEA) design can simultaneously enhance phase stability, refine the microstructure, and optimize material properties.
generation.material_initial_state: A multi-principal element alloy (e.g., an Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti or similar HEA system) with potentially multiple phases and unrefined microstructure when designed without targeted computational guidance.
generation.intervention: Use a CALPHAD-based high-throughput calculation (HTC) approach to screen a wide compositional space and processing parameters, targeting desired single-phase solid solution formation and specific precipitate fractions.
generation.conditions: Computational screening across a defined composition range (e.g., 5–50 at.% per element) and temperature conditions representative of both fabrication and service environments, with subsequent experimental validation under identical processing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Stabilized phase diagram predictions that indicate a dominant solid solution phase with a controlled amount (e.g., 5–50 vol%) of strengthening precipitates (such as L2₁ or ordered B2 phases) acting as microstructural mediators.
generation.mechanism: By leveraging thermodynamic databases and simulation, the CALPHAD method predicts the balance between mixing entropy and enthalpy contributions, thereby guiding alloy composition and processing routes that reduce unwanted phase formation while promoting fine microstructure and optimal mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEAs designed using this method will display improved high-temperature phase stability, a refined and more homogeneous microstructure with minimal detrimental phases, and enhanced mechanical properties such as higher yield strength and ductility compared to conventionally designed HEAs.
generation.baseline: HEAs developed without such computational guidance may exhibit multiple phases, coarser microstructures, and suboptimal properties due to non-optimized compositional and processing parameters.
generation.boundary: The extent of improvement may be limited by the accuracy of existing thermodynamic databases, especially for higher-order (>5 elements) systems, and by the scaling challenges in computational time and experimental reproducibility.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvements in property metrics (e.g., strength increments or grain-size reduction percentages) remain uncertain without extensive experimental validation, and potential discrepancies may arise due to database limitations.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of HEA samples with similar targeted nominal compositions. One group is designed using a CALPHAD-based HTC screening to determine optimal compositions and processing parameters, and the other is designed without such computational guidance (using traditional trial-and-error methods). Both groups are processed under identical conditions. Compare the phase formation, microstructure (e.g., grain size and phase homogeneity), and mechanical properties (such as yield strength and ductility) at service-relevant temperatures.
measurements: Phase identification via XRD and electron microscopy
Grain size and microstructural homogeneity via SEM/TEM
Mechanical testing (e.g., tensile/compression tests) at elevated temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CALPHAD-designed HEA samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in phase stability (single-phase or targeted precipitate formation), microstructure refinement, and mechanical properties compared to the conventionally designed samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The design stage of the quinary HEA started with the calculation of the thermophysical parameters, mainly enthalpy of mixing (∆ H mix ), entropy of mixing ( Δ S mix ), atomic size difference ( δ ), and the omega parameter ( Ω ) for several compositions. The ability of a material to form a single-phase was empirically shown to depend on these three parameters. For that, the value for Δ H mix was recommended to be in the range of −15 to 5 kJ per mole, while δ should be smaller than 6.6 and Ω larger than 1.1 [26] , [27] . ∆ H mix , δ , and Ω were then calculated using Eqs. 1 – 4 respectively. Other theoretical parameters such as density ( ρ ), melting temperature ( T m ), and VEC were calculated using the rule of mixture, as shown in Eq. 5 , where i represents the element type, X represents the property, r is the atomic radius, and c represents the concentration of element i .

The atomic radii and enthalpy used in the calculations are taken from refs. [28] , [29] , respectively. The concept of HEAs provides us an unprecedented degree of freedom in the design of advanced alloys with promising properties. For the rapid exploration of the vast compositional space and investigation of the composition and temperature effects on the microstructure, advanced HEA-design strategies and efficient tools are necessary. At present, a few advanced HEA-design strategies were reported by combining the physicochemical criteria, CALPHAD, data mining, and multi-objective optimization algorithm [21] , [22] , [35] – [37] , demonstrating that the CALPHAD method has played an important role in the design of advanced HEAs. There are two essential requirements to carry out calculations, using the CALPHAD method: computational software and database.

The computational software could significantly affect the efficiency of HTC since massive calculations are carried out. In the example of the Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system, it takes only a few hours on a desktop computer to finish the HTCs (~ 3 × 10 3 ) within the composition range of 5–50 at.% for each element and finally screen out eight potential alloys.
